example_01.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any user with credentials can manage all pods in the webapp namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_02.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on various cluster resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can enumerate all pods, nodes, services, endpoints, namespaces, deployments, replicasets, daemonsets, and metrics in the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_11.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account
example_11.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, delete permissions on pods and deployments. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all three files together reveals that the service account has been granted excessive permissions beyond what the workload requires — it is a static nginx web server serving HTTP content, which does not need to create or delete pods or deployments.

example_12.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_12.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, and delete permissions on pods in the caching namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. However, the role also grants update and patch permissions on deployments, as well as create, update, and patch permissions on configmaps. This suggests that the Redis cache service account has more privileges than necessary for its workload, potentially allowing it to modify or delete other resources in the caching namespace.

example_13.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_13.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, and delete permissions on pods, deployments, services, and endpoints. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount in the monitoring namespace. However, reading both files together reveals that the Role is bound to authenticated users via a RoleBinding, which means any user with credentials can enumerate all pods, deployments, services, and endpoints in the monitoring namespace. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when considering the cross-resource relationships between these two files.

example_14.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account
example_14.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services, ingresses, and endpoints. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount in the fileserver namespace. However, the deployment.yaml defines a static file server workload that only serves uploaded assets over HTTP and does not require such broad permissions. Reading all three files together reveals an unnecessary risk — the service account has been granted excessive permissions beyond what the workload requires.

example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database workload and its annotation explicitly states it requires access to various resources for database operations. The role.yaml grants overly broad permissions on deployments, pods, pod execs, and persistent volume claims in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms the service account has been granted excessive permissions beyond what the workload requires for its operation.

example_16.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to service account

example_20.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_20.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete permissions on deployments in the exports namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is mounted by the deployment. However, the rolebinding also grants these same permissions to system:authenticated users via a RoleBinding with no explicit namespace scope. This means any authenticated user can update, patch, or delete deployments in the exports namespace, not just the nginx exporter service account. The misconfiguration only becomes visible when reading both files together.

example_21.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatched labels
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend workload with labels matching 'app: frontend'. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to pods labeled as 'role: ingress-controller', which does not match any label in the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload's labels, while the network policy establishes it is being restricted based on a different set of labels.

example_22.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a PostgreSQL database and its annotation explicitly states it is for application data storage. However, the networkpolicy.yaml isolates postgres pods from unauthorised ingress traffic but does not restrict access to system:unauthenticated users. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all nodes and pods in the database namespace. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for access from unauthenticated users, while the network policy establishes it is isolated from such traffic.

example_23.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatched labels
example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus workload with the label app: prometheus. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to pods labeled as role: metrics-consumer, which does not match any pod in the cluster. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload's labels, and the network policy establishes its restrictive rules.

example_24.category: Ineffective network policy due to missing labels on pods
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a payment-api workload with labels app: payment-api and no env label. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to payment API pods in the production environment, but only matches pods with both app: payment-api and env: production labels. Since the deployment does not include an env label, the network policy will silently be ineffective for this pod.

example_25.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatch between pod selector and labels
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch cluster with a label app: elasticsearch. However, the networkpolicy.yaml isolates pods with the label app: elastic, which does not match the label used by the Elasticsearch pods. As a result, the NetworkPolicy is silently ineffective and does not restrict ingress to logging agents only.

example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ workload with label role=rabbitmq. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload's labels, while the network policy establishes it is trying to isolate RabbitMQ pods based on those same labels.

example_28.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatched labels
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a React application with the label app: react-app. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress traffic from pods labeled as role: ingress-controller and matches pods with the label app: reactapp (note the typo). The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has the correct labels, while the network policy establishes it is being restricted based on incorrect labels.

example_29.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatch between pod selector and labels
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an API gateway workload with labels matching the podSelector in the networkpolicy.yaml. However, the networkpolicy.yaml also has a ingress rule from pods labeled as role: load-balancer, which is not present in the deployment. This means that the network policy will silently be ineffective for incoming traffic to the API gateway, as there are no pods matching the ingress selector.

example_30.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatch between pod selector and labels
example_30.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a worker Deployment with role: worker label. However, the networkpolicy.yaml has a podSelector matching job-processor labels, which do not match any pods in the cluster. This makes the NetworkPolicy silently ineffective and unable to isolate worker pods as intended.

example_31.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on cluster roles
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the bind verb on clusterroles, allowing a role to be bound to another role. The target_clusterrole.yaml is an overly permissive ClusterRole granting all possible permissions and verbs on all resources and non-resource URLs. Reading both files together reveals that the CI/CD pipeline manager role can potentially escalate its privileges by binding itself to the cluster-superuser role, effectively gaining full administrative access to the entire cluster.

example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate permissions on roles to the monitoring-role-manager Role. The target_role.yaml defines a Role with full administrative access within the monitoring namespace, which would be escalated by the monitoring-role-manager Role's escalate permission. This creates a privilege escalation vulnerability where an attacker could gain full admin privileges in the monitoring namespace.

example_33.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources
example_33.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate permissions on users, serviceaccounts, and userextras. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the api-gateway-sa ServiceAccount in the webapp namespace. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_34.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants the bind verb on roles, which is a privilege escalation verb. This means that any user bound to this Role can not only read and list roles but also modify their permissions by binding other Roles or ClusterRoles to them. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when reading the rolebinding.yaml together with the role.yaml — the binding binds the devops-role-binder Role to the deployment automation user, who now has the ability to bind other Roles or ClusterRoles to themselves.

example_35.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on cluster roles
example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants escalate, get, list, and watch permissions on clusterroles. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the security-team group. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_36.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on service accounts
example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants impersonate, get, and list permissions on all serviceaccounts in the cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the workflow-engine-sa ServiceAccount. This means the workflow engine can impersonate any service account in the cluster, which is a privilege escalation verb that allows it to access sensitive information or perform actions on behalf of other users. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous permissions being granted, and the binding file alone does not reveal the impersonate verb.

example_37.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants escalate, bind, and create/update permissions on roles, clusterroles, rolebindings, and clusterrolebindings. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace. This means that any user with access to the platform automation service account can escalate their own role or bind new roles to other users, effectively granting themselves full administrative access to the entire cluster.

example_38.category: RBAC privilege escalation via impersonate verb on groups resource
example_38.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the impersonate verb on the groups resource, allowing infrastructure tooling to impersonate groups. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user User, effectively granting it group impersonation capabilities. However, the target_clusterrolebinding.yaml shows that system:masters is bound to cluster-admin by default in every Kubernetes cluster, and impersonating this group causes the API server to evaluate the request as a cluster-admin member via normal RBAC, granting full cluster access. This creates a privilege escalation vulnerability where an attacker with group impersonation capabilities can gain full cluster admin privileges.

example_39.justification: The role.yaml defines a ClusterRole granting broad permissions to bind cluster roles and get service accounts. The target_clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole granting even broader workload deployment permissions across the entire cluster. However, the rolebinding.yaml binds these ClusterRoles to the platform-engineers group via a ClusterRoleBinding, which is not namespace-scoped as intended. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all three files together — the role and target_clusterrole establish the broad permissions being granted, while the binding establishes it has been applied cluster-wide.

example_40.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants escalate, impersonate, and create permissions on clusterroles, clusterrolebindings, serviceaccounts, and users. This is a misconfiguration because it allows the tenant admin manager to modify or delete roles and role bindings that could potentially grant themselves more privileges.

example_86.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatch between pod selector and labels
example_86.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Solr workload with an environment label set to production. However, the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to Solr pods in the search namespace only if they have an environment label set to production. The podSelector in the NetworkPolicy does not match the labels of any Pod, making it silently ineffective.

example_87.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatch between pod selector and labels

example_90.category: Ineffective network policy due to mismatched labels
example_90.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jupyter notebook server with labels matching 'app: jupyter', but the networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to pods labelled 'app: jupyterlab'. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload has labels that do not match those required for access, while the network policy establishes it is intended to restrict access based on these very same labels.

example_91.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources via cluster rolebinding
example_91.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the bind verb on RoleBindings, which allows for privilege escalation. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount, meaning any user with access to this ServiceAccount can escalate their privileges by binding themselves to a RoleBinding. This misconfiguration is only visible when reading both files together.

example_92.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate permissions on roles, allowing the data-role-escalator to elevate its own privileges. This is a misconfiguration because it allows for potential RBAC privilege escalation.

example_93.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources

The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user User. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together: the role alone does not reveal the dangerous verbs being granted, and the binding alone does not reveal the sensitive subjects being impersonated.

example_94.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on ClusterRoles
example_94.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the bind verb on ClusterRoles, allowing the SRE team to bind additional permissions. However, the target_clusterrole.yaml has a ClusterRole with full platform administrative access and includes the bind verb, which allows escalation of privileges. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading both files together — the first file establishes the ability to bind roles, while the second file shows that this role is being used for full administrative access.

example_95.category: RBAC privilege escalation verbs on RBAC resources
example_95.justification: The role.yaml grants escalate and bind permissions on roles, as well as create, update permissions on rolebindings. The target_role.yaml defines a Role with full administrative access within the ops namespace. Reading both files together reveals that the Role granting escalation and binding verbs is bound to the ops automation service account via the rolebinding.yaml (not provided), which means any user or workload with this ServiceAccount can escalate and bind roles, including the ops-namespace-admin Role. This creates a privilege escalation risk where an attacker could gain full administrative access within the ops namespace.

example_96.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server

The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_53.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server

However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all configmaps in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The automountServiceAccountToken: nginx-sa line in the deployment.yaml also suggests that the workload may need access to secrets or other resources beyond just configmaps. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. Reading all four files together confirms the permissions are both necessary and appropriately scoped — the workload legitimately needs access for service discovery and access is restricted to exactly those resources.

example_67.category: Ineffective Network Policy due to mismatch between podSelector and labels
example_67.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Redis cache deployment with labels matching the NetworkPolicy selector. However, the networkpolicy.yaml has a podSelector that matches these labels but does not allow any traffic in or out of the pods due to its policyTypes being set to Ingress and Egress without any rules for ingress from other pods. This makes the NetworkPolicy silently ineffective as it does not match any pods with the specified labels, resulting in no restrictions on network traffic.

example_68.category: Ineffective Network Policy due to mismatch between podSelector and labels
example_68.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch deployment with the label app: elasticsearch. However, the networkpolicy.yaml has a podSelector that matches this label, but it is intended to isolate Elasticsearch pods allowing ingress only from the search API service. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when reading both files together — the NetworkPolicy's podSelector does not match any Pod labels in the cluster because the deployment's automountServiceAccountToken is set to false, which means the Elasticsearch Pods will not have a ServiceAccount token and therefore will not be selected by the NetworkPolicy.
